newsitem.title: USA: Swiss official pledges fast probe of Jewish assets.
newsitem.headline: Swiss official pledges fast probe of Jewish assets.

text.p: A Swiss official said on Wednesday his government would move swiftly to trace assets left in Swiss banks by Jews and other Holocaust victims, saying Switzerland knew "our reputation as an honourable country ... is at stake."

"It is our intention and expectation that we will conclude our investigation within two to three years," Thomas Borer, head of a Swiss task force coordinating the investigation, testified at a hearing of the U.S. House of Representatives Banking Committee.

"Let me make it clear at the outset: nothing is more important to the people and government of Switzerland than establishing the complete truth in this matter as swiftly and humanely as possible," Borer said in his opening statement.
"We are fully aware that nothing less than our reputation as an honourable country and reliable friend is at stake."
The Swiss parliament on Monday gave final approval for a study of Swiss financial dealings with Nazi Germany and the fate of Jewish assets.

Borer was testifying by invitation before the House committee, whose chairman, Iowa Republican Jim Leach, said as the panel began its hearings on Wednesday: "The motivation of this committee is desire for full disclosure, for justice to be wrought: nothing more or less."

Borer said that if it was found that assets belonging to Holocaust victims were still being held wrongfully in Switzerland, the Swiss government would make every effort to return them to their rightful owners.
If the owners could not be traced, he said, Switzerland would make the money available to "relevant charities."
Borer said that the new Swiss law setting up the investigation would lift banking and other professional secrecy laws for five years.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican whose constituents include a strong Jewish voting bloc, also testified at the House hearing and accused Swiss banks of betraying the trust of Jews and others who deposited their assets to protect them from the Nazis.

"The Swiss banks invited and encouraged Jews and other presecuted peoples to entrust funds and family valuables to them for safekeeping. It becomes clearer now that this trust has been betrayed," said D'Amato, whose own Senate committee has also been investigating the issue.
"The tragic story of the Swiss bankers' insensitivity and indifference to the plight of these victimised people is heartwrenching," the senator said.
"I know that the Swiss people, proud of their country's reputation as a neutral country, are as shocked as much as anyone else by the emerging record of Swiss complicity with the Nazis."

Former U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker, who is chairing an independent committee to investigate dormant or heirless Swiss bank accounts deposited by persons fearing Nazi persecution, said it would be hard to make a complete record.
"The practical difficulties revolve around the sheer length of time -- 50 to 60 years -- since the time the accounts originated," Volcker said.
His committee includes three members from the Swiss Bankers Association and three members chosen by the World Jewish Congress.
